messages.subject: General Workflow question
parts:
Hi all,
I'm doing an analysis with Cardinal2 but I have doubts because I'm not sure I'm doing it in the proper way. Could this general workflow be valid for a study?

1. Load imzML data
2. Processing steps: normalization (rms), smoothing, and baseline reduction
3. Filter (mzFilter) preprocessed dataset. I'm doing this to reduce he remaining small/noisy peaks
4. Peak picking (for use in other classification/prediction or clustering analysis)
5. Binning over peak picked dataset (this is my main doubt) for posterior dataset combine

As I said, my main doubt is where to apply binning because I need to combine all datasets in order to have the same mz range when doing the statistical analysis

Any suggestions? 
Regards, 
Edu

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: General Workflow question
parts:
The proposed workflow looks fine to me.

The typical suggestion we've been using is to do peak picking on a subset of the data (say, every tenth spectrum or so), to develop an overall peak list, and then bin everything to that peak list. If you have a consensus list of peaks, it should be straightforward to combine those datasets after binning to the peaks, as they would then be MSContinuousImagingExperiment objects with the same m/z values..

Any MSProcessedImagingExperiment objects (which are produced during peak picking) can be combined relatively easily by updating their m/z-values (which are already being binned to some extent) to a common sequence.

The biggest issue is if you want to do classification cross-validation, which can be biased if the peak list comes from the full dataset. The crossValidate() method provides some ability to separately pre-process each CV fold, but this hasn't been heavily tested or documented yet.

I mean to write up some more detailed examples, but haven't found the time yet.

-Kylie

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: General Workflow question
parts:
peakAlign() must come after peakPick(), as it assumes the data has been reduced to peaks.

The issue is that both peakAlign() and peakBin() require a list of reference peaks -- peakAlign() will calculate from the mean spectrum if missing, and peakBin() requires it explicitly. These references are taken from the whole dataset, so if you later do cross-validation, your training subsets will include some peak information influenced by the test subsets.

There are two main approaches to pre-processing we support, and the new crossValidate() method supports both via setting the .process=TRUE argument.

1. Use peakPick() %>% peakAlign() %>% peakFilter() on the whole dataset and use whatever peaks were detected. This is the simplest, least time-consuming approach, but it also risks losing information. Peaks that aren't detected in a particular spectrum will have intensities of 0, even if their intensities are not exactly 0. How much of an impact on the downstream analysis this may have will vary depending on how good the peak detection was. . . crossValidate() supports this approach by providing a dataset that has been peakPick()ed, but NOT aligned yet. It will then individually peakAlign each training subset and align each test subset to the peaks from the corresponding training subset.

2. Use peakPick() %>% peakAlign() %>% peakFilter() on a sample of the dataset, and then peakBin() the full spectrum dataset to those peaks. This method is a little more time-consuming (and potentially requires storing more intermediate datasets), but it should be more robust for downstream analysis, as less information is lost. Summarized intensities should be more accurate, since it doesn't rely on peakPick() getting everything right the first time. . . crossValidate() supports this approach by providing a spectra-processed but NOT peak-picked dataset as '.x' AND a peak-picked (but unaligned) version of the same dataset to '.peaks'. It then peakAlign()s the peak-picked versions for each training subset, and peakBin()s each training/test subset to those peaks.

Both of these approaches avoid using any information from the whole dataset in the training subsets, with the cost of being a good bit more time-consuming to do.

Supporting this kind of processing within crossValidate() was one of the last new features I added to version 2.2 before it was released, so I haven't been able to thoroughly test it yet. Improving support for this kind of workflow, working out any bugs, and adding documentation is on my to-do list for Bioconductor 3.10.

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: General Workflow question
parts:
Unfortunately, I don't yet really have a way to do pre-processing for cross-validation that is both fast and efficient and also statistically unbiased.

Unless you have a predetermined list of known reference peaks that you can use. (Just give that to peakBin(). This is the ideal scenario.)

Or if you don't actually need to keep the mass resolution and can just bin to arbitrary features. (Just use mzBin(). This can be fine if you're only interested in classification accuracy and don't really need to determine influential mass features.)
